questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms as used in genetics:

(i) Lethal gene.

(ii) Codominance.

(iii) Incomplete dominance. *[9 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Lethal gene.** A gene (allele) whose expression **causes the death of the organism** that carries it, usually before it reaches reproductive age (often at the embryo stage). Most lethal alleles are **recessive** and kill only the homozygous recessive (e.g. sickle-cell anaemia in its homozygous form, cystic fibrosis); some are **dominant** (e.g. the allele for Huntington's disease, which acts late in life). A lethal allele changes the expected Mendelian ratios, e.g. a 2 : 1 ratio in place of 3 : 1 because one class of zygotes dies. Examples: yellow coat colour in mice (homozygous yellow die in the uterus); the frizzled-feather gene considered in this question.

**(ii) Codominance.** The situation in which **two different alleles of a gene are both fully expressed in the heterozygote**, neither being dominant over the other, so the phenotype shows both characters side by side. Example: the human **ABO blood groups**, where $I^A$ and $I^B$ are codominant: a person $I^AI^B$ has blood group AB with both antigens on the red cells. Another example: roan cattle (red and white hairs together) from red $\times$ white parents.

**(iii) Incomplete dominance (partial or blending dominance).** The situation in which **neither allele is completely dominant** and the **heterozygote has a phenotype intermediate** between those of the two homozygotes. Example: in snapdragon (*Antirrhinum*) or four o'clock plant (*Mirabilis*), red $\times$ white gives pink $F_1$; crossing two pink plants gives red, pink and white in the ratio **1 : 2 : 1** (phenotypic ratio equal to the genotypic ratio). The difference from codominance is that the heterozygote shows a blend and not both parental characters.

questions.enonce_markdown: The nature of the feather in birds is either normal or frizzled. Birds with homozygous dominant frizzled feathers die because of their inability to maintain their body temperature. Using genetic symbols and diagrams, show what will be the outcomes between two frizzled feathered birds. *[9 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Genetic symbols.** Frizzled is dominant, so let **F** = allele for frizzled feathers and **f** = allele for normal feathers.

- $FF$: frizzled homozygote, **dies** (cannot keep its body temperature).
- $Ff$: frizzled, survives.
- $ff$: normal feathers, survives.

Frizzled birds that live to breed cannot be $FF$, so **both parents are heterozygous, $Ff$**.

**Cross**

| | |
|---|---|
| Parental phenotypes | Frizzled $\times$ Frizzled |
| Parental genotypes | $Ff$ $\times$ $Ff$ |
| Gametes | $F$ or $f$ $\times$ $F$ or $f$ |

**Punnett square**

| | $F$ | $f$ |
|---|---|---|
| $F$ | $FF$ (dies) | $Ff$ (frizzled) |
| $f$ | $Ff$ (frizzled) | $ff$ (normal) |

**Outcome**

- Expected genotypes of the fertilised eggs: $1\,FF : 2\,Ff : 1\,ff$.
- The $FF$ birds (one quarter) **die**, so among the **surviving birds** the genotypes are $2\,Ff : 1\,ff$.
- Phenotypes of the survivors: **2 frizzled : 1 normal** (about two-thirds frizzled and one-third normal).
- For example, of 12 fertilised eggs: 3 $FF$ (die), 6 $Ff$ (frizzled), 3 $ff$ (normal); 9 chicks survive.

Normal feathered birds breed true ($ff \times ff$ gives only normal birds); frizzled birds never breed true, since a frizzled $\times$ frizzled cross always gives some normal chicks.

questions.enonce_markdown: Why do the above results deviate from the normal Mendelian ratio? *[2 marks]* *(9, 9, 2 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown: The normal Mendelian ratio for a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes is **3 : 1** (phenotypes) and 1 : 2 : 1 (genotypes). Here the ratio is **2 : 1** because the **dominant frizzled allele is lethal in the homozygous condition**: the $FF$ zygotes (one quarter of the offspring) die, so that class is **missing** from the progeny and the three-quarters expected to be frizzled is reduced to two-thirds of the survivors.
